entry.title: A Rigorous, Tractable Measure of Model Complexity

link.title: A Rigorous, Tractable Measure of Model Complexity

entry.content:
An accurate assessment of a model’s complexity is crucial for topics such as interpretation, generalization, and model selection. However, existing complexity measures either rely on heuristic assumptions or are computationally prohibitive. In this paper, we present a mathematically rigorous yet easy-to-compute measure of model complexity that is based on the similarities between feature vectors for different inputs. It is thus well-defined for any parametric model (via NTK feature generalization) and for kernel-based non-parametric models (via the induced kernel). We prove that our measure of complexity generalizes model-specific complexity measures, including polynomial degree (for polynomial regression), kernel length scale (for Mat'ern kernels), number of neighbors (for k-nearest neighbors), number of splits (for decision trees), and number of trees (for random forests). We also use our measure to obtain new insights into the double descent phenomenon for random Fourier features, random forests, neural networks, and gradient boosting.

entry.title: A Unified Framework for Training-Dataset Aggregation and Exact Machine Unlearning via Gibbs Probability Measures

link.title: A Unified Framework for Training-Dataset Aggregation and Exact Machine Unlearning via Gibbs Probability Measures

entry.content:
In this paper, three operations on Gibbs probability measures are studied: renormalization, normalized log-linear combination, and nesting. The resulting measures are shown to be Gibbs probability measures with explicit expressions for their objective functions, reference measures, and regularization factors. These measures are further characterized as unique solutions to optimization problems involving linear combinations of the original objective functions, subject to either relative entropy regularization or relative entropy constraints. When the reference measures are probability measures, geometric interpretations of these three operations are established involving Pythagorean identities and exponential geodesics.A central result is the equivalence between nesting and normalized log-linear combinations of Gibbs probability measures. These results are then applied to supervised machine learning with Gibbs algorithms, which are represented by Gibbs probability measures. In this context, either through nesting or log-linear combinations, Gibbs algorithms trained on local datasets are used to form new Gibbs algorithms trained upon the aggregation of all local training datasets. Interestingly, the parameters of such operations, determine the weights of each training data point on the aggregated dataset. %Operations on local Gibbs probability measures are shown to control the contributions of training data. This observation is leveraged for achieving: (a) exact machine unlearning in centralized, decentralized, and federated learning systems; and (b) centralized-equivalent performance, in the sense of producing algorithms trained on the aggregation of all local datasets in decentralized and federated learning .

entry.title: A covariance density for a point process and a random field

link.title: A covariance density for a point process and a random field

entry.content:
The spatial point process literature offers a well-developed theory for characterizing covariances within a point process or between different point processes using joint intensity functions or cross joint intensity functions. However, similar summary statistics are missing for characterizing the covariance between a point process and a random field. We introduce a normalized mixed covariance density that fills this gap for covariances between variables of a random field and linear functionals of a point process. We construct a non-parametric kernel estimator of the covariance density and a data-driven method for bandwidth selection. We further use our estimate of the covariance density to test the dependence between a point process and a random field. Several existing tests require observations of the random field at the events of the point process. These are often not available when the random field is sampled on a grid unrelated to the point process. Then interpolation is needed to impute random field values at point process events. Our covariance density estimate in contrast does not require interpolation. We investigate the performance of our non-parametric estimator and the method for bandwidth selection in applications to simulated and real data.

entry.title: A latent space hidden Markov model for clustering views in longitudinal multilayer networks

link.title: A latent space hidden Markov model for clustering views in longitudinal multilayer networks

entry.content:
We propose a Bayesian latent space model for clustering longitudinal multilayer networks in which network slices are represented by a finite set of recurrent latent regimes, each associated with a regime-specific latent geometric configuration. Layer-specific hidden Markov chains govern regime membership through a parsimonious additive transition model, allowing heterogeneous temporal dynamics across relational dimensions while sharing a common set of latent configurations. Edge weights are modelled using a Hurdle Negative Binomial distribution, accommodating both excess zeros and overdispersion in weighted networks. An optional sender-receiver extension further captures persistent node-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study demonstrates that the proposed model can accurately recover both latent regimes and their associated configurations, with recovery performance depending on the degree of regimes’ similarity. We also assess the robustness of the proposed method under model misspecification. Applications to GDELT geopolitical event and European Parliament roll-call voting data demonstrate the flexibility of the framework across diverse domains.

entry.title: Algorithmic Principles For Multiclass Learning Are Hard To Come By: Limits of Regularization and Proper Learning

link.title: Algorithmic Principles For Multiclass Learning Are Hard To Come By: Limits of Regularization and Proper Learning

entry.content:
Two of the most fundamental questions in statistical learning theory are the following: which prediction problems are learnable, and how should they be learned? For the former, elegant answers often take the form of combinatorial dimensions. The latter question, however, has proved considerably more elusive: all known general-purpose multiclass learners rely on intricate orientations of exponentially large one-inclusion structures, and familiar algorithmic principles such as proper learning and regularization remain poorly understood. Motivated by prior work, we ask whether learning reduces to proper learning—possibly over a larger hypothesis class—and whether proper or improper multiclass learning can ultimately be captured by suitable regularizers. Our primary results answer both questions negatively, resolving three open problems from prior work. First, we exhibit a learnable multiclass problem that cannot be embedded in any properly learnable class, meaning learning cannot be reduced to proper learning by enlarging the hypothesis class. Second, we demonstrate that proper learning can require training error and characterize this phenomenon precisely: every properly learnable class admits a proper learner making $o(m)$ errors on samples of size $m$, but every prescribed sublinear scale $a_m=o(m)$ is necessary for some properly learnable problem. Third, regularization is not a general learner: we exhibit a properly learnable class that cannot be learned by any Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) learner, and a learnable class that cannot be learned by any local regularizer. We complement these impossibility results with a positive theory that gives two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and characterizes SRM representability through integrability of revealed preferences.

entry.title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI

link.title: Alignment Myopia in Generative AI

entry.content:
Current generative AI alignment relies on a myopic paradigm that prioritizes immediate conversational satisfaction. By relying on short-horizon feedback, this approach ignores the profound, longitudinal externalities of persistent human-AI interaction, which can lead to adverse outcomes such as cognitive atrophy, social erosion, and diminished human agency. To address this, we propose a paradigm shift toward long-horizon alignment that accounts for how AI reshapes human experience over time. To this end, we map the tensions between near-term utility and long-term costs of AI use across four facets of human well-being to reveal outcomes that current reward models fail to capture. Ultimately, we advocate for moving beyond simple preference optimization toward alignment strategies that actively foster long-term human well-being by navigating these complex temporal scales.

entry.title: All reweighted paths lead to Rome: Unification of reweighting schemes for stratified path sampling

link.title: All reweighted paths lead to Rome: Unification of reweighting schemes for stratified path sampling

entry.content:
Path sampling-based stratification algorithms such as Transition Interface Sampling (TIS) enable the evaluation of kinetic rate constants and mechanisms of complex molecular rare event transitions. By sampling only short dynamical trajectories, TIS allows constructing an estimate of the unbiased dynamics by reweighting the interface path ensembles. In the past decades several methods have been developed and applied to achieve such path reweighting, based on statistically optimal use of the trajectory data. Why and how this reweighting exactly works has been underexplored up to now. Here we discuss several different schemes to compute the reweighted path ensemble (RPE), notably point-wise matching, Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM), Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio (MBAR), variance based reweighting (VBR) and survival analysis reweighting (SAR). We show that except for the point-wise matching the other methods are leading to the same outcome, and in fact can be seen as identical. Moreover, the SAR links to a well-established nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimator of product-limit form. This allows a synthesis of all path reweighting schemes, identifying the common underlying nature. All schemes follow from this common origin. We illustrate the reweighting with some simple examples, and show that care has to be taken when applying WHAM, if the number of interfaces and histogram bins do not match.

entry.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction

link.title: A low-rank decoder bottleneck bounds reliability in foundation-model perturbation prediction

entry.content:
Foundation-model predictors of perturbation response are evaluated primarily by aggregate accuracy. Using their predictions to prioritize experiments requires assessing each prediction’s reliability. We audit the state-transition (ST) decoder used in STATE across three encoders (SE-600M, scGPT, and Tahoe-x1) and four cell lines under CRISPRi. The decoder’s first attention layer has a low-rank output. Projecting this output onto 4-32 fixed directions estimated from training activations preserves mean per-perturbation Pearson delta correlation (PDC). This low-rank attention bottleneck bounds the decoder’s reliability by distance to training responses: PDC declines as the cosine distance from a perturbation’s observed response to its nearest training response increases. We propose predicted-NN-distance, the cosine distance from a predicted response to its nearest training response, as a per-prediction confidence score. The score has a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.81 with PDC, close to the 0.88 obtained with the observed response. Thresholds calibrated on this score transfer across encoders and cell lines, and the score remains predictive of PDC for drug perturbations.

entry.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy

link.title: An Exact Poisson Mixture Representation of Siler Remaining Life Expectancy

entry.content:
The Siler model describes mortality from birth to old age as the sum of a declining immaturity hazard, a constant background hazard, and an increasing senescence hazard. No standard closed form is available for its remaining life expectancy, which must therefore be evaluated by numerical integration. We show that Siler remaining life expectancy at age $x$ is a Poisson mixture of Gompertz-Makeham remaining life expectancies, that is, a Poisson-weighted average of life expectancies in models with only a constant background hazard and an exponentially increasing senescence hazard. All components share the senescence hazard. Their background hazards increase from one component to the next by the rate at which immaturity mortality declines. The Poisson mean is the immaturity hazard that remains to be accumulated after age $x$. This representation yields an exact series of generalized exponential integrals with a closed-form bound on the truncation error. Replacing the background hazard by its discounted counterpart also gives the Laplace transform of the remaining lifetime. The mixture bounds the life expectancy lost to immaturity mortality: up to a term below the reciprocal of $a_2+b_1$, this loss equals the probability of an immaturity death times the life expectancy with the immaturity hazard removed. In annual Siler fits to Swedish female mortality, we estimate that the loss at birth fell from 4.3 years in 1900 to less than 0.01 years in 2020, which accounts for 15% of the gain in life expectancy at birth over the period.

entry.title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case

link.title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case

entry.content:
Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength, and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal’s meaning depends on the others: high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses. The proposed Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes such dependencies as four interpretable interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. We evaluate it on 55 acquisitions assisted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 2008-2024 by acquirers with a parent listed in the United States. Six financial inputs come from regulatory reports published before each failure; two deal terms, which the winning bidder knows when it bids but investors learn at the announcement, come from the regulator’s press releases. The outcome, a positive three-day abnormal return around the announcement, records the market’s initial reception, not realized success. Under grouped, nested cross-validation, the Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression on the same inputs and 0.632 for ridge regression; permutation tests that repeat the full model selection give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark. Thresholds tuned for the F1 score approve most acquisitions with negative returns and realize negative utility when each costs three times what a positively received acquisition gains.

entry.title: Anchor PCA

link.title: Anchor PCA

entry.content:
Principal component analysis (PCA) is one of the most widely used unsupervised dimension reduction techniques. We study PCA for data from multiple related domains. Since principal components generally differ across domains, one way to obtain a shared low-rank embedding is to perform PCA on the pooled data. However, this approach can focus on spurious directions that exhibit high variation in only a few domains. To find a robust embedding that still explains most variance in unseen but similar domains, we propose instead to focus on shared directions of variation. To this end, we introduce Anchor PCA which trades off overall explained variance with agreement between the shared and domain-specific low-rank embeddings. Anchor PCA amounts to PCA on a modified target matrix and thus can be solved efficiently. Moreover, we show that Anchor PCA recovers a maximal invariant subspace and admits a minimax reconstruction interpretation under bounded domain-specific covariance inflations. On simulated and real-world data with temporal distribution shift, we demonstrate, respectively, that Anchor PCA recovers the maximal invariant subspace and yields embeddings that explain more variance on unseen domains than the pooling baseline and a worst-case alternative. Taken together, these findings establish Anchor PCA as a promising approach to robust unsupervised dimension reduction from multi-domain data.

entry.title: AutoEnergyDesign: An LLM-Driven Agent for Automatic Energy System Design Optimization

link.title: AutoEnergyDesign: An LLM-Driven Agent for Automatic Energy System Design Optimization

entry.content:
The design optimization of building energy systems represents a complex, high-dimensional search problem involving discrete technology selections, continuous sizing parameters, and intricate economic trade-offs in which every candidate must be evaluated by a year-long simulation. This paper presents AutoEnergyDesign, in which a Large Language Model (LLM) agent reasons over past simulation results, proposes configuration changes and learns in context from each outcome, while a git-based mechanism reverts changes that do not improve the design. The agent couples a reasoning model with explicit memories, a constrained action interface, and an environment-grounded keep/revert feedback signal. The simulator covers eight technologies and computes the 25-year Net Present Cost (NPC). On a case study with measured building loads, the agent, instantiated with three Claude models (Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5; ten runs of 50 simulations each), is compared with random search, Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) Bayesian optimization and a (1+1) evolution strategy that shares the agent’s acceptance rule (ten seeds of 300 evaluations). With all three models the agent reaches an NPC of 3.53MEUR, 1.20% and 0.23% below the best results of TPE and of the evolution strategy, and comes within 1% of it after a median of 18 to 27.5 simulations; among the baselines, only the evolution strategy does so, after a median of 192 evaluations. Every decision is recorded, making the search auditable.

entry.title: Balance-Guided Forest for Causal Effect Estimation

link.title: Balance-Guided Forest for Causal Effect Estimation

entry.content:
Covariate balancing is widely used for estimating causal effects in observational studies. A central challenge is determining which covariate features should be balanced. Forest-kernel balancing provides a data-driven way to learn informative balancing features. Existing forest-kernel balancing methods first learn a tree-based representation and then construct balancing weights. However, this procedure creates a mismatch, as limited tree capacity may be spent on features that are already well represented. We propose Balance-Guided Forest (BGF), which uses the current balancing weights to guide subsequent tree construction. BGF grows trees using a novel splitting score that combines residual imbalance with an outcome contrast, favoring splits that separate outcome-relevant regions where imbalance remains. This couples representation learning with covariate balancing rather than treating balancing as a downstream step. We establish an oracle-type bound that links the iterative construction to weighting error and causal bias. Simulations exhibit improvements in causal estimation relative to existing forest-kernel approaches. Real-data applications illustrate the practical behavior of BGF across observational studies.

entry.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Global-local Clustering of High-dimensional Functions

link.title: Bayesian Nonparametric Global-local Clustering of High-dimensional Functions

entry.content:
There is a rich literature on clustering functional data with applications to time-series modeling, trajectory data, and even spatiotemporal applications. Existing methods are classified into two categories of global clustering that assigns an identical membership over the whole domain, and local clustering that allows multiple memberships based on the sub-domains. Classical literature has typically focused on global clustering that may struggle with degenerate clustering or produce numerous spurious clusters for high-dimensional functions. In contrast, a limited number of local clustering approaches have been proposed that are not scalable to high-dimensional functions and have limited theoretical guarantees. Focusing on basis expansions for high-dimensional functions, we propose a novel global-local framework that partitions coefficients into exclusive subsets and imposes independent Dirichlet process priors on each subset. The proposed framework reduces the total number of possible clustering configurations compared to local clustering and therefore provides greater scalability, while simultaneously providing enhanced flexibility compared to global clustering by relaxing the assumption of identical clustering for all elements in the high-dimensional function. Moreover, the proposed method incorporates spatially correlated errors to provide better model fitting and shows posterior consistency properties that asymptotically recover the true density of random functions. An efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm is developed for implementation. Extensive simulations involving images illustrate the improved scalability, clustering, and function estimation under the proposed method compared to classical approaches. We apply the proposed approach to a spatial transcriptomics application where the goal is to infer clusters of genes with distinct spatial patterns of expressions.

entry.title: Bayesian Superpopulation Models for Population-Based Diabetes Surveillance Using Multi-Site Electronic Health Record Data

link.title: Bayesian Superpopulation Models for Population-Based Diabetes Surveillance Using Multi-Site Electronic Health Record Data

entry.content:
Electronic health records (EHRs) are increasingly used for disease surveillance. However, data collected in EHRs may not be a representative sample of the target population for inference. Methods for EHR-based surveillance remain in their nascence. In addition to simple weighting approaches, researchers have used multilevel regression and poststratification (MRP), a popular technique for finite population quantity estimation that remains understudied in EHRs. We are motivated by a US-based collaborative to modernize diabetes surveillance using EHR data from different health system centers across the country. To estimate type 1 diabetes (T1D) prevalence in children and adolescents, we propose and evaluate three Bayesian superpopulation models that are distinguished by how they account for two important features of EHR data: unobserved heterogeneity and data sparsity. The three models include an analysis of variance-inspired approach; a model with geographic effects varying by demographic subgroup; and MRP, which we consider as the reference model. We apply the models to estimate prevalence overall and in demographic- and geographic-based subgroups. Using plasmode simulations, we evaluate model estimation performance while preserving the complexity of the EHR data. Our results show that the superpopulation-based prevalence estimates were higher than those observed in the EHR sample alone, with the magnitude of the differences varying by health system center. The bias and coverage probabilities of MRP markedly worsened when the EHR sample size was smaller or the selection mechanism was more complex. Overall, the superpopulation model based on analysis of variance demonstrated the best estimation performance.

entry.title: Community detection with the Bethe-Hessian

link.title: Community detection with the Bethe-Hessian

entry.content:
The Bethe-Hessian matrix, introduced by Saade, Krzakala, and Zdeborov'a (2014), is a Hermitian matrix designed for applying spectral clustering algorithms to sparse networks. Rather than employing a non-symmetric and high-dimensional non-backtracking operator, a spectral method based on the Bethe-Hessian matrix is conjectured to also reach the Kesten-Stigum detection threshold in the sparse stochastic block model (SBM). We provide the first rigorous analysis of the Bethe-Hessian spectral method in the SBM under both the bounded expected degree and the growing degree regimes. Specifically, we demonstrate that: (i) When the expected degree $d\geq 2$, the number of negative outliers of the Bethe-Hessian matrix can consistently estimate the number of blocks above the Kesten-Stigum threshold, thus confirming a conjecture from Saade, Krzakala, and Zdeborov'a (2014) for $d\geq 2$. (ii) For sufficiently large $d$, its eigenvectors can be used to achieve weak recovery. (iii) As $d\to\infty$, we establish the concentration of the locations of its negative outlier eigenvalues, and weak consistency can be achieved via a spectral method based on the Bethe-Hessian matrix.

entry.title: Conjugate priors for Bayesian Variable Selection in exponential family Generalized Linear Models

link.title: Conjugate priors for Bayesian Variable Selection in exponential family Generalized Linear Models

entry.content:
Covariate selection in Generalized Linear Models (GLMs) is a fundamental problem in statistics, as including irrelevant predictors might lead to overfitting and poor interpretability, while omitting relevant ones might result in biased estimates. Most Bayesian approaches to variable selection – including spike-and-slab priors and continuous shrinkage priors – have key limitations, e.g., (i) are based on non fully conjugate formulations, (ii) are restricted to a linear model, or (iii) lack posterior consistency guarantees for the variable selection procedure and model parameters. In this work, we propose a fully Bayesian hierarchical and conjugate framework for covariate selection in GLMs, applicable to any distribution in the exponential family, based on modeling a binary inclusion indicator that directly encodes covariate inclusion in the linear predictor. In our approach, variable selection and parameter estimation are performed simultaneously, incorporating both sources of uncertainty in posterior inference. Consequently, our methodology provides a valid post-model Bayesian selection procedure. We present theoretical guarantees of the proposed fully conjugate Bayesian variable selection for GLMs, establishing posterior consistency of both the inclusion indicators and the active regression coefficients. We derive an efficient Gibbs Sampling algorithm with a corresponding R package implementation. We validate the proposed method on synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating competitive predictive and inferential performance.

entry.title: Conservative neural posterior estimation via distributionally robust training

link.title: Conservative neural posterior estimation via distributionally robust training

entry.content:
Simulation-based inference with neural posterior estimation (NPE) often yields overconfident and unreliable posteriors under limited simulation budgets. To address this, we propose DRO-NPE, a distributionally robust approach that replaces the standard NPE objective with a worst-case loss over a Wasserstein ambiguity set. We introduce KL-based metrics for miscoverage and miscalibration, and use these to show that the DRO-NPE objective controls overfitting and reduces posterior overconfidence. Our method is tractable, parallelisable, and readily integrates with standard normalising flows. Across benchmark SBI tasks, DRO-NPE consistently improves coverage and calibration, while narrowing the gap between empirical and population NPE loss, leading to more reliable inference in low-simulation regimes.

entry.title: Covariate Adjustment for Time-Restricted Marginal Win Statistics in Randomized Trials: Assumption-Lean Inference and Guaranteed Efficiency Gain

link.title: Covariate Adjustment for Time-Restricted Marginal Win Statistics in Randomized Trials: Assumption-Lean Inference and Guaranteed Efficiency Gain

entry.content:
Hierarchical composite endpoints, analyzed through win statistics such as the net benefit (NB), win ratio (WR), and win odds (WO), are increasingly used in randomized trials to prioritize endpoints according to clinical importance. Although covariate-adjustment methods for win statistics have been developed, a unified model-assisted approach for mixed-type, time-restricted HCEs with simultaneous asymptotic no-loss efficiency guarantees remains of interest. We propose a unified, model-assisted covariate-adjustment framework for time-restricted marginal win statistics evaluated at a prespecified post-randomization restriction horizon, a clinically interpretable estimand particularly suited to acute and high-acuity trials with well-defined short-term follow-up windows. The Hoeffding–H’ajek projection of the two-sample win–loss U-statistics yields subject-level influence functions for the marginal win and loss probabilities. We apply treatment-specific linear covariate adjustment to these influence functions and propagate the adjustment to NB, log WR, and log WO. The resulting estimators are assumption-lean, remaining consistent and asymptotically valid without correct specification of the linear working model, and are asymptotically guaranteed efficiency gain over their unadjusted counterparts. Simulations with mixed-type HCEs demonstrate substantial efficiency and power gains with prognostic covariate adjustment. However, including additional non-prognostic covariates can impair finite-sample variance estimation and inflate Type I error, particularly in smaller trials. Bootstrap variance estimation improved inferential calibration in these settings. We illustrate the proposed method using a randomized acute kidney injury alert trial.

entry.title: Curvature-Calibrated Quasi-Bayesian Updating for Moment-Restricted Models

link.title: Curvature-Calibrated Quasi-Bayesian Updating for Moment-Restricted Models

entry.content:
Quadratic moment-based quasi-posteriors depend on a weighting matrix governing both the contributions of moment conditions and the scale of posterior uncertainty. We propose curvature-calibrated quasi-Bayesian (CCQB) updating, which iteratively evaluates the inverse of the estimated moment covariance (or long-run covariance) at the center of the resulting fixed-weight quasi-posterior. A two-part stopping rule monitors changes in the center and Monte Carlo error in estimating it. Under local regularity conditions, the ideal calibration map is contractive, and its fixed point is root-N consistent. The calibrated quasi-posterior and the sampling distribution of its center have the inverse Godambe information matrix as their root-N-scale covariance. Simulations show substantial gains over identity weighting. Further iteration has little effect in linear designs but improves calibration for some parameters in nonlinear settings, although nominal coverage is not uniformly achieved. An application to longitudinal childhood wheeze data illustrates the method under within-subject dependence.

entry.title: Decoupling Distance and Networks: Hybrid Graph Attention-Geostatistical Methods for Spatio-temporal Risk Mapping

link.title: Decoupling Distance and Networks: Hybrid Graph Attention-Geostatistical Methods for Spatio-temporal Risk Mapping

entry.content:
Accurate spatial prediction and rigorous uncertainty quantification are central to modern spatial epidemiology and environmental risk analysis. We introduce a statistically principled hybrid modelling framework that integrates the nonlinear, attention-based representation learning capabilities of a dynamic Graph Attention Network (GATv2) with a latent Gaussian spatial process from model-based geostatistics (MBG). This framework jointly captures relational dependence encoded in graph structures and continuous spatial dependence governed by physical proximity. We evaluate the proposed model via a controlled simulation study and an applied analysis of malaria prevalence data, comparing its predictive accuracy, calibration, and uncertainty quantification against classical geostatistical models and standalone GATv2 architectures. Our analyses show that GATv2 captures complex nonlinear interactions but fails to account for residual spatial autocorrelation, resulting in miscalibrated predictive distributions. Conversely, geostatistical models provide coherent uncertainty quantification through structured covariance functions yet are constrained by linear predictor assumptions and by their reliance on Euclidean distance to encode spatial structure. By integrating attention mechanisms and nonlinear features with an explicit probabilistic spatial random field, the hybrid model captured the relational dependence, consistently improved predictive accuracy, and provided more realistic uncertainty quantification in both simulation and applied settings. Overall, the findings demonstrate that the hybrid model constitutes a statistically coherent and empirically robust framework for modelling complex spatial and spatio-temporal processes in settings where both distance-based and structure-based dependencies operate.

entry.title: Diffusion Models Observe Only Gradients: A Geometric Perspective on Score Matching Errors

link.title: Diffusion Models Observe Only Gradients: A Geometric Perspective on Score Matching Errors

entry.content:
Score-based diffusion models are typically trained by minimizing the $L^2$ score matching error, and standard theoretical analyses rely on this quantity to bound the sampling discrepancy between the learned and target distributions. Recent work has shown that the score admits an orthogonal decomposition into gradient and solenoidal components in which only the gradient part matters for exact sampling. We apply this decomposition to the score error of trained models and study its quantitative consequences. Since only the gradient component of the error enters the marginal Fokker-Planck dynamics, a model can incur arbitrarily large $L^2$ score error while perfectly matching the target. Starting from this observation, we present three results. First, we derive an upper bound on the Kullback-Leibler divergence that depends only on the observable gradient component of the error. It tightens the standard Girsanov bound for generic score networks and identifies that bound’s looseness as the cost of working with path-space rather than marginal-space dynamics. Second, we prove that no non-trivial function of the $L^2$ score error can uniformly lower bound any divergence between the learned and target distributions. Third, we give an estimator of the gradient component, computable from denoising score matching residuals via a dual Sobolev identity, which empirically correlates substantially better with sample quality than the full $L^2$ error.

entry.title: Discovering like a scientist: Literature-informed dimensionless learning for physical closure of data-driven equations

link.title: Discovering like a scientist: Literature-informed dimensionless learning for physical closure of data-driven equations

entry.content:
Data-driven methods can recover compact equations, yet the physical dependence of their coefficients across operating conditions often remains unresolved. Dimensionless groups can explain this variation, but selecting relevant groups from the many dimensionally admissible combinations remains challenging. Here, we introduce a knowledge-guided framework for dimensionless learning, called {\pi}-former. It learns patterns of variable association and exponent assignment from a corpus of 1,288 established dimensionless groups. Under exact dimensional constraints, the model proposes interpretable basic groups whose combinations are optimized against observations. Across seven physical problems, the framework identifies predictive dimensionless coordinates within seconds. Integration with equation discovery further expresses condition-dependent coefficients through these coordinates, recovering established physical scalings in multi-condition simulations. Applied to experimental measurements of evaporation-driven wetting, the framework discovers dimensionless coordinates and uses them to construct a unified trajectory equation. The resulting model generalizes to held-out conditions across liquids and initial volumes, outperforming existing empirical models. These results establish dimensionless learning as a transferable bridge between accumulated scientific knowledge and data-driven equation discovery, enabling artificial intelligence to uncover physically meaningful laws from observations.

entry.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials

link.title: Does Your Trial Simulator Know What the Drug Does? An Intervention-Blind Test of Interventional Validity on 7,207 Registered Trials

entry.content:
Patient world models are increasingly proposed as simulators of clinical trials, and recent surveys rank their capabilities on a ladder from temporal prediction to counterfactual rollouts. Position on that ladder is currently assigned by reading papers rather than by measurement. We turn the counterfactual rung into a measured quantity. From 30,119 completed phase 2/3 trials with results posted to ClinicalTrials.gov we construct 9,996 audited within-trial contrasts from 7,207 trials, and we score a simulator on how much of its accuracy depends on knowing which intervention was tested. The instrument is an intervention-blind reference: the same model, trained on the same trials, with every intervention-identifying field withheld. Interventional skill is the error the full model removes relative to that reference. On a temporal split (878 test contrasts from 655 trials) a registry-trained gradient-boosting simulator removes a fifth of the error of a trivial baseline, but its interventional skill is -0.12 (95% CI -0.21 to -0.05): withholding the intervention makes it better, and no alternative featurisation, stratum, temporal cut or same-molecule retrieval yields an interval above zero. A frontier language model reading only the registered protocol has interventional skill 0.20 [0.08, 0.31]; smaller and open-weight models sit at the limit of detection. Perturbation tests show the large model uses the intervention as such: swapping the arms reverses the sign of its prediction in 86% of contrasts. The blind reference is itself not drug-blind (a language model recovers the withheld drug class 45% of the time from the blind prompt), so interventional skill is a conservative lower bound. A reliability layer shows that ranking by predicted error lowers it but that calibrated error control does not transfer under temporal shift. Benchmark, code, prompts and per-call model outputs are released.

entry.title: Doubly robust win statistics for hierarchical survival endpoints in individual- and cluster-randomized trials

link.title: Doubly robust win statistics for hierarchical survival endpoints in individual- and cluster-randomized trials

entry.content:
Prioritized composite endpoints compare trial participants according to a prespecified clinical hierarchy, and the win estimands are increasingly used to summarize treatment effects. When the component event times are right-censored, a pairwise comparison may remain unresolved, and treating unresolved pairs as ties yields a win statistic whose value depends on the censoring distribution. We define win, loss, and tie probabilities at a fixed restriction time for prioritized time-to-event outcomes in individual-randomized trials and extend them to cluster-randomized trials, where cluster-average and individual-average estimands assign equal weight to clusters and to participants, respectively. We propose doubly robust estimators that combine inverse probability of censoring weighting with joint outcome models to incorporate information recorded before censoring. Under covariate-dependent censoring, the resulting U-statistics are consistent when either the censoring models or joint outcome models are correctly specified for both treatment arms, but not necessarily both. We establish asymptotic normality and derive analytic variance estimators for computationally efficient inference. Simulation studies under both designs evaluate bias, precision, and confidence interval coverage under working model misspecification. Applications to two real-world studies demonstrate the use of the proposed methods under individual- and cluster-randomized trials.

entry.title: Dynamic Strategy Selection

link.title: Dynamic Strategy Selection

entry.content:
We consider the problem of dynamically selecting among competing strategies using observable predictors. To mitigate estimation noise and excessive switching, we regularise the estimated policy with a switching cost, which may exceed actual transaction costs when these are too small to provide sufficient regularisation. Since switching costs make current choices affect future decisions, we formulate the problem using dynamic programming. The optimal policy is estimated using a reinforcement learning algorithm based on iterated regressions, making the procedure simple to implement. We apply the method to monthly rotation among momentum, value, profitability, and defensive U.S. equity factors over a sample of about 60 years. Using a parsimonious set of state variables, the estimated policy outperforms both the myopic dynamic policy and the best fixed factor in hindsight in out-of-sample evaluation. Under weak conditions, we show theoretically that the decision rule estimated from empirical data is asymptotically consistent for the unknown optimal decision rule. Simulation results illustrate the finite-sample relevance of these asymptotic results.

entry.title: ESS-Flow: Training-free guidance as Bayesian inference in source space

link.title: ESS-Flow: Training-free guidance as Bayesian inference in source space

entry.content:
Guiding pretrained flow-based generative models for conditional generation or to produce samples with desired target properties enables solving diverse tasks without retraining on paired data. We present ESS-Flow, a gradient-free method that leverages the Gaussian prior of the source distribution in flow-based models to perform Bayesian inference directly in the source space using elliptical slice sampling. ESS-Flow only requires forward passes through the generative model and observation process, making it applicable even when gradients are unavailable, such as with non-differentiable simulation-based observations or quantization in the generation process. We demonstrate its effectiveness on scientific applications including generating materials with target properties, protein backbone structures with improved designability, and synthesizable, drug-like molecules.

entry.title: Efficient Gaussian Process Modeling for Large Replicated and Censored Data in Industrial Research

link.title: Efficient Gaussian Process Modeling for Large Replicated and Censored Data in Industrial Research

entry.content:
Gaussian process regression is widely used for modeling responses in both physical and computer experiments. In practice, data from physical experiments may include replications and be subject to censoring due to equipment limitations or contextual constraints, and such datasets can be large, posing a scalability challenge for standard Gaussian process inference. Motivated by a real-world industrial research study, we develop a Gaussian process modeling framework that efficiently analyzes large replicated and censored data. Our approach integrates a Vecchia approximation for computational scalability with a likelihood-based formulation that fully exploits replication and rigorously incorporates information from censored observations, analogous to exact simulation from truncated distributions. Through experiments on synthetic data and a real case study from industrial research, we demonstrate that the proposed method yields improved predictive accuracy and reliable uncertainty quantification compared to existing approaches, making it well suited for large-scale applications with structured replication and incomplete data.

entry.title: Efficient Robust Learning at the Information-Theoretic Limit

link.title: Efficient Robust Learning at the Information-Theoretic Limit

entry.content:
In an important recent work, Blanc (2026) gave an algorithm for robustly learning Boolean concept classes with respect to a fixed distribution that outputs a (randomized) classifier achieving the optimal error of $\eta + \varepsilon$ where $\eta$ is the noise rate. In contrast, it is well known that deterministic hypotheses cannot achieve error less than $2\eta + \varepsilon$. Blanc’s algorithm is computationally inefficient, and the main problem left open in his work is to find a polynomial-time algorithm given access to an oracle for empirical risk minimization (ERM). Here we resolve this problem and give such an algorithm. Additionally, we give an efficient algorithm (no ERM oracle required) for robustly learning any function class that admits low-degree polynomial approximators with respect to hypercontractive distributions. This captures basic settings including halfspaces with respect to Gaussian marginals. Our techniques make new connections to various types of online convex optimization algorithms. As a surprising consequence, we show that efficient SQ learnability in the agnostic setting implies efficient learning with contamination (with respect to Gaussians or uniform over the hypercube).

entry.title: Efficient estimation of regression models for recurrent events in presence of terminal events

link.title: Efficient estimation of regression models for recurrent events in presence of terminal events

entry.content:
Recurrent events are common in biomedical studies, and efficient methods are needed to analyse them, particularly when a terminal event may occur. Regression modelling of the marginal mean of recurrent events provides a simply interpretable approach, but standard estimation based on inverse probability of censoring weighting may not fully exploit observed event histories in multiple events settings. We demonstrate how the popular Ghosh-Lin proportional means model can be estimated efficiently by developing an augmentation procedure that is also applicable to composite endpoints. Using semiparametric efficiency theory, we characterize the fully efficient estimator. First, we investigate its construction under frailty models. We then propose a dynamic censoring-augmented estimator that is straightforward to compute and does not require a fully specified joint model for recurrent and terminal events. We show theoretically that it improves on the standard Ghosh-Lin estimator and derive an explicit expression for its asymptotic variance reduction. We also establish conditions under which tests of no treatment effect remain valid in randomized trials when the proportional means model is misspecified. Extensive simulations examine performance under dependence between recurrent and terminal events, unobserved heterogeneity, censoring-model misspecification, and auxiliary covariates. The practical gain of the proposed methods is illustrated with an analysis of catheter-related bloodstream infections in patients with chronic intestinal failure receiving home parenteral support.

entry.title: Estimating Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning

link.title: Estimating Implicit Regularization in Deep Learning

entry.content:
Deep learning systems are known to exhibit implicit regularization (alt. implicit bias), favoring simple solutions instead of merely minimizing the loss function. In some cases, we can analytically derive the implicit regularization – connecting it to an equivalent penalty that augments the learning objective. However, modern deep learning systems are complex, carrying modifications to the training procedure and architecture (e.g. early stopping, minibatching, dropout) whose effects are not always directly interpretable. Although estimating the resulting implicit regularization could aid theorists in algorithm design and practitioners in interpreting their hyperparameter choices, this problem has received little direct attention. It is also tractable: regularization makes weight updates deviate from loss gradients, promising a signal for identifying implicit bias. Here we provide gradient matching methods that can be used to empirically estimate the implicit regularization. Our method works on networks with known regularization, recovering popular explicit penalties like $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$. It also replicates known implicit effects, like the quadratic weight penalty induced by early stopping in gradient descent, demonstrating that it can be used to test theories of implicit regularization. Crucially, because our method is empirical, it can handle implicit regularization in arbitrary networks. We demonstrate this use by characterizing implicit $\ell_2$ effects of dropout in deep networks. Our work shows that practitioners can use gradient matching to understand regularization in networks with implicit biases that are too complicated to derive analytically.

link.title: Exact signal recovery from generative priors with sigmoid output activation

entry.content:
We show exact signal recovery in generative compressed sensing for feedforward neural networks with piecewise-linear activations and a final sigmoid activation, with no assumption of expansivity. Consider a ReLU network of depth $d$ with a sigmoid final activation, whose input layer, of dimension $k$, is the narrowest, and let $K$ be the geometric mean of the widths of its layers. We show that, with high probability, all signals of the range whose entries lie in $[\delta, 1 - \delta]$ are uniformly recovered from $m \gtrsim k(d \log(K/k) + \log(1+\log(1/\delta)))$ measurements.

entry.title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights

link.title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights

entry.content:
Large language models excel at factual recall, yet the fundamental limits of storing input–output associations with neural networks remain unclear. We study these limits in a minimal setting: a linear associative memory that maps $p$ input embeddings in $\mathbb{R}^d$ to their $d$-dimensional targets via a linear layer, requiring each mapped input to score its own target above all other outputs. Since all inputs compete for the same outputs, these constraints are strongly correlated, which makes the storage capacity $p_c$ — the largest number of associations that can be stored — hard to characterise. We address this in three steps. First, we introduce a decoupled model, in which each input competes with its own independent set of outputs, and provide numerical and analytical evidence that it is equivalent to the original model, both in capacity and in the structure of the learnt solution. Second, using tools from statistical physics, we show that the decoupled model has capacity $p_c \log p_c / d^2 = 1/2$, extend this computation to linear two-layer networks, and go beyond the capacity by predicting the spectrum of the learnt weights and the storage mechanism. The latter explains how the optimal solution outperforms a na"ive Hebbian rule: rather than boosting input–output alignments with broad fluctuations, it raises the correct scores just above the extreme-value threshold set by the competing outputs. Third, we prove the decoupled model’s capacity thresholds rigorously, including in the non-convex two-layer case; combined with a recent proof for the original model, this shows that both models have the same capacity for full-rank weights. These findings give a sharp characterisation of factual storage in linear networks, and suggest decoupling as a general tool for memorisation and learning problems in which each input must be matched to one of an extensive number of outputs.

entry.title: Finite-width shift of the edge of chaos in deep neural networks

link.title: Finite-width shift of the edge of chaos in deep neural networks

entry.content:
Deep neural networks train best when they are initialised at the edge of chaos, the critical line in the plane of weight and bias variances on which the distance between two inputs neither grows nor shrinks with depth. The line is known for infinitely wide networks; at finite width it moves, and how it moves has been disputed. We treat the logarithm of the distance between two inputs through a network of width $N$ as a random walk and compute its drift and variance to order $1/N$. The edge of chaos moves to a larger weight variance, by $\Delta\sigma_w^2=-a_1/(N\,\partial_{\sigma_w^2}\ln\chi_1)$, about $8/N$ for $\tanh$ networks at a bias variance of $0.05$, confirmed by simulations of the exact finite-width recursion. The shift describes a typical network; the average over many networks is dominated by rare networks in which the distance grows, and its critical point moves the other way, which explains why calculations and simulations have disagreed. Backpropagation follows the same random walk, so the shift applies to gradients unchanged. Along the edge of chaos, the information about the similarity of two inputs is constant until the compression over the depth exceeds about one nat, which fixes where to sit on the line. The results give an initialisation rule, Crinit, that places a network on its finite-width edge of chaos without a search. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST at width $64$ it is more accurate than the standard rules at their usual settings, by a small margin in shallow networks and a large one in deep networks, where most standard rules fail; it trains in fewer steps, and it matches or beats the standard rules with a tuned gain.

entry.title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes

link.title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes

entry.content:
Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical framework for event sequence data, with applications spanning seismology, social media, and electronic health records. Recently, neural TPPs have been reported to substantially outperform classical TPPs, such as Hawkes processes, but these comparisons pitted flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted form, and did not consider large-scale medical data. Here, we revisit this comparison through a systematic evaluation of Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs, on five established benchmark datasets and on two large-scale medical evaluation tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records, under autoregressive next-event prediction. First, the previously reported gap between Hawkes processes and neural TPPs largely disappears once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels. Second, the flexibility of the intensity parametrization also limits prior neural TPPs: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and is on par with the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into a time term $\log p(t)$ and a type term $\log p(d \mid t)$, we find that this flexibility advantage lies almost entirely in the time density: more flexibility does not improve the type term. On these benchmarks, the gains of neural TPPs thus lie mostly in modeling when events occur, not which. Third, our results underscore the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs: only on the MIMIC-IV ICU records do neural TPPs retain an advantage in the type term. Our results inform both future method development and model choice. We release our framework, TorchPP, as an open-source package with consistent implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

entry.title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players

link.title: Follow or Surpass? Collaboration, Sound, and the Recognition of Influence in Lineages of Jazz Trumpet Players

entry.content:
Cultural fields cohere not only horizontally, through collaboration, but also vertically, through lineages of artistic influence. Considerable attention has been devoted to collaboration networks in various fields of creative production; however, we know less about the structure of artistic influence that is nevertheless key to individual artistic development and the evolution of genres. We examine the structure of such an influence network in a genealogy of 52 prominent jazz trumpet players, combining musicians’ discographies, demographic characteristics, geographical locations, and audio analysis of more than 16,000 recordings with exponential random graph models. Direct collaboration, overlap in collaborators, and sonic context similarity, that is, the similarity of the recordings on which players appear, are each associated with an ascribed influence tie, net of the others. Not surprisingly, ascribed ties connect musicians whose recordings share a similar sonic context, but musicians also tend to collaborate with their influences and share collaborators with them. However, players whose recordings share a sonic context and who move in the same circle of collaborators can be thought of as peers or rivals, rather than as influences of each other, because lineage implies a succession predicated on difference as much as on continuity. Taken together, our findings suggest that a field’s account of its own evolution is neither a record of who played together nor a map of shared sonic contexts, but a selective ordering that requires both. While our data do not permit a causal account, our aim is to provide a rich and varied methodological strategy and descriptive as well as inferential tools to understand the yet understudied vertical integration of cultural fields through influence ties.

entry.title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects

link.title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects

entry.content:
Structural Causal Models and Bayesian Networks are the dominant framework for representing causal relations. They are fundamentally type-level formalisms since their estimands, Average Treatment Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effects, are properties of distributions over populations, not of individual units. When treatment effects exhibit unbounded heterogeneity, these estimands collapse. What persists is the structural, token-level core of causation. We argue that Petri Nets under the Individual Token Philosophy are the natural representation of these token-level causal structures. We develop a formal translation from Bayesian Networks to Petri Nets, providing a two-layer account of individualized causality. The PN layer provides a structural representation of causal mechanisms that does not rest on distributional assumptions. entry.title: Fréchet Regression on the Bures-Wasserstein Manifold

link.title: Fréchet Regression on the Bures-Wasserstein Manifold

entry.content:
Fr'echet regression, or conditional Barycenters, is a flexible framework for modeling relationships between covariates (usually Euclidean) and response variables on general metric spaces, e.g., probability distributions or positive definite matrices. However, in contrast to classical barycenter problems, computing conditional counterparts in many non-Euclidean spaces remains an open challenge, as they yield non-convex optimization problems with an affine structure. In this work, we study the existence and computation of conditional barycenters, specifically in the space of positive-definite matrices with the Bures-Wasserstein metric. We provide a sufficient condition for the existence of a minimizer of the conditional barycenter problem that characterizes the regression range of extrapolation. Moreover, we further characterize the optimization landscape, proving that under this condition, the objective is free of local maxima. Additionally, we develop a projection-free and provably correct algorithm for the approximate computation of first-order stationary points. Finally, we provide a stochastic reformulation that enables the use of off-the-shelf stochastic Riemannian optimization methods for large-scale setups. Numerical experiments validate the performance of the proposed methods on regression problems of real-world biological networks and on large-scale synthetic Diffusion Tensor Imaging problems.

entry.title: Fundamental Limits of Coherent Imaging in The Presence of Atmospheric Turbulence

link.title: Fundamental Limits of Coherent Imaging in The Presence of Atmospheric Turbulence

entry.content:
We study the fundamental limits of jointly estimating the signal amplitude and the atmospheric phase distortion in complex-valued multi-look coherent imaging, where the measurements are corrupted by multiplicative speckle and additive Gaussian noise, all looks share a known Gaussian sensing matrix, and both parameters belong to structured classes. By analyzing a constrained maximum likelihood estimator, we establish an upper bound on the joint minimax risk that holds uniformly over the admissible parameter classes, while oracle reductions and Fano-type arguments yield worst-case lower bounds over the admissible parameter classes. These results quantify the effects of structural complexity, signal and measurement dimensions, the number of looks, and the noise level, and establish matching minimax rates in several settings, with a remaining gap for phase estimation at low noise when the measurement dimension exceeds the signal dimension. We also construct a two-stage estimator for signal recovery under arbitrary diagonal sign distortions in the real-valued analogue. Under additional conditions, it recovers the signs up to a global sign with high probability and yields a uniform signal risk bound without a distortion-complexity term. Numerical experiments illustrate the dependence of the joint, signal, and phase errors on the model parameters and provide further support for the theoretical analysis.

link.title: Generalized Hyperrectangular Prediction Sets in Multivariate Conformal Prediction

entry.content:
In multivariate conformal prediction, many nonconformity scores yield prediction sets with complex geometry (e.g., ellipsoids or density level sets) that are difficult to interpret and visualize. Hyperrectangles offer a practical alternative by providing one interval per output. We extend this notion to Cartesian products of arbitrary one-dimensional sets, which we call generalized hyperrectangles. We introduce a rectangularization framework that turns any continuous multivariate nonconformity score, or conditional density, into one yielding generalized hyperrectangular prediction sets with finite-sample coverage. We establish key geometric properties of our rectangularization framework and provide useful intuitions on generalized hyperrectangles. We further establish a representation theorem showing that a broad class of hyperrectangular conformal methods based on max-aggregated coordinate-wise scores can be interpreted as rectangularizations of implicit conditional densities. Through synthetic and real-world experiments, we quantify the efficiency cost of rectangularization, while highlighting its benefits, especially for practical applications of uncertainty quantification.

entry.title: Generalized and Scalable Deep Gaussian Process Emulation

link.title: Generalized and Scalable Deep Gaussian Process Emulation

entry.content:
Gaussian process (GP) emulators have become essential tools for approximating complex simulators, significantly reducing computational demands in optimization, sensitivity analysis, and model calibration. While traditional GP emulators effectively model continuous and Gaussian-distributed simulator outputs with homogeneous variability, they typically struggle with discrete, heteroskedastic Gaussian, or non-Gaussian data, limiting their applicability to increasingly common stochastic simulators. A scalable Generalized Deep Gaussian Process (GDGP) emulation framework is introduced to accommodate simulators with heteroskedastic Gaussian outputs and a wide range of non-Gaussian response distributions, including Poisson, negative binomial, and categorical distributions. The GDGP framework leverages the expressiveness of DGPs and extends them to latent GP structures, enabling it to capture the complex, non-stationary behavior inherent in many simulators while also modeling non-Gaussian simulator outputs. GDGP is made scalable by incorporating the Vecchia approximation for settings with a large number of input locations, while also developing efficient inference procedures for handling large numbers of replicates. In particular, methodological developments are presented that further enhance the computation of the approach for heteroskedastic Gaussian responses. A series of synthetic and empirical examples demonstrates that these extensions deliver the practical application of GDGP emulators and a unified methodology capable of addressing diverse modeling challenges. The proposed GDGP framework is implemented in the open-source R package dgpsi.

entry.title: Generative Modeling for Cascading Extremes via Autoregressive Transformers

link.title: Generative Modeling for Cascading Extremes via Autoregressive Transformers

entry.content:
Extreme events often occur sequentially, from earthquake-tsunami cascades to successive extreme losses in financial markets. We introduce an extremal token representation that encodes multivariate observations as a categorical sequence. A quiet token records the absence of threshold exceedances; otherwise, the token identifies the exceeding component with the largest marginal probability-scale score. The representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations. It preserves the identity and temporal ordering of dominant exceedances but discards their magnitudes and the identities of nondominant simultaneous exceedances. A decoder-only transformer estimates the history-dependent next-token kernel on this representation, and recursive sampling generates future token sequences from the induced joint predictive law. We amortize our generative model by pretraining across simulated process families with varying parameters and dependence persistence. Next-token predictions are evaluated against exact conditional probabilities for held-out categorical processes and particle filter references for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. Applied to ten-second returns for five semiconductor stocks, the pretrained model supports zero-shot transfer, while a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement between observed and generated token frequencies and transition patterns. These results support task-specific tokenization and simulation-based pretraining for modeling which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes.

entry.title: Geometric ergodicity of the block Gibbs sampler for Bayesian linear mixed models with scale mixtures of normal random effects

link.title: Geometric ergodicity of the block Gibbs sampler for Bayesian linear mixed models with scale mixtures of normal random effects

entry.content:
We study a Bayesian linear mixed model whose random effects follow a scale mixture of normal distributions with an arbitrary mixing distribution, a class that contains the Student-t, slash, contaminated normal, normal-generalized inverse Gaussian and Laplace laws. Conditionally conjugate priors lead to a three-block Gibbs sampler that alternates between the variance components, the latent precision weights, and the regression coefficients together with the random effects. Using a drift function built from fractional powers, we give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity of this chain, which involve a moment of the mixing distribution of some order larger than 1/2 and its behaviour near the origin. An equivariance of the sampler under rescaling of the design then shows that the conditions hold for all the families above, including Student-t random effects with any degrees of freedom, for every random-effects design matrix, full rank or not, with the rank entering only the conditions on the priors of the variance components. Together with posterior moment bounds, geometric ergodicity justifies Monte Carlo standard errors and effective-sample-size stopping rules for the regression coefficients and the log-variance components. Simulations examine these procedures at practical run lengths: joint confidence regions need a correction for the number of batches, and under sequential stopping their observed coverage remains slightly below the nominal level. We illustrate the methods with longitudinal beta-HCG measurements from early pregnancies, in which the latent weights reveal larger between-subject variability among abnormal pregnancies.

entry.title: Goal-Oriented Sequential Bayesian Experimental Design for Causal Learning

link.title: Goal-Oriented Sequential Bayesian Experimental Design for Causal Learning

entry.content:
We present GO-CBED, a goal-oriented Bayesian framework for sequential causal experimental design. Unlike conventional approaches that select interventions aimed at inferring the full causal model, GO-CBED directly maximizes the expected information gain (EIG) on user-specified causal quantities of interest, enabling more targeted and efficient experimentation. The framework is both non-myopic, optimizing over entire intervention sequences, and goal-oriented, targeting only model aspects relevant to the causal query. To address the intractability of exact EIG computation, we introduce a variational lower bound estimator, optimized jointly through a transformer-based policy network and normalizing flow-based variational posteriors. The resulting policy enables real-time decision-making via an amortized network. We demonstrate that GO-CBED consistently outperforms existing baselines across various causal reasoning and discovery tasks-including synthetic structural causal models and semi-synthetic gene regulatory networks-particularly in settings with limited experimental budgets and complex causal mechanisms. Our results highlight the benefits of aligning experimental design objectives with specific research goals and of forward-looking sequential planning.

link.title: High-dimensional Four-Level Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis for Unbalanced Level Data with Application to Concussion Data

entry.content:
We implement the Structured Functional Principal Component Analysis (SFPCA) framework of Shou et al. (2015) in a four-level nested setting with arbitrarily unbalanced group sizes at every level of the hierarchy. While the SFPCA framework can in principle accommodate deeper hierarchical structures, practical implementations remain challenging when the number of curves is large and the hierarchy is highly unbalanced. Our contributions are twofold. First, we operationalize SFPCA for four hierarchical levels with arbitrary unbalancedness across units. Second, we propose a memory-efficient computational strategy that makes the analysis of large collections of curves feasible on conventional hardware. In particular, we construct the four design-specific matrices required for the Method of Moments (MoM) estimators of the level-specific covariance operators while controlling their memory footprint, which would otherwise grow prohibitively with the number of curves. We illustrate the approach using three subsets of the NCAA-DoD Grand Alliance Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium dataset (2014-2017).

entry.title: Impossibility of Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Individual Treatment Effects

link.title: Impossibility of Distribution-Free Predictive Inference for Individual Treatment Effects

entry.content:
Uncertainty quantification for individual treatment effects (ITEs) is a daunting challenge in causal inference. Motivated by recent advances in conformal prediction, several works aim to construct distribution-free prediction sets for ITEs with desired coverage under standard assumptions such as strong ignorability and overlap. In this paper, we show that such goals are fundamentally unattainable. Specifically, we establish finite-sample and asymptotic impossibility results demonstrating that any distribution-free prediction set achieving desired coverage for ITEs must be trivial, in the sense that it has infinite expected length. This infinite-expected-length conclusion requires no regularity assumption on the covariates and holds even in their absence. Our analysis builds on ideas from the hardness of conditional independence testing and exploits the missing-data nature of causal inference. These results provide a new perspective on existing methods, clarifying that their apparent success necessarily relies on additional structural assumptions beyond standard causal assumptions.

entry.title: Inference on the Reliability Function with Type-I Censored Weibull Data

link.title: Inference on the Reliability Function with Type-I Censored Weibull Data

entry.content:
Reliability inference based on parametric distributions is an important problem in electrical and mechanical engineering. Most existing methods rely on approximations or bootstrap procedures, which may not perform satisfactorily when data are censored or sample sizes are small. Hence, there is an urgent need to develop exact inference approaches for these situations. This article introduces a new approach for deriving exact parametric tests and confidence intervals for distributions such as the lognormal, loglogistic, and Weibull. We revisit several issues in classical reliability analysis based on the survival function. Because lifetime data are often censored in practice, the proposed approach is designed for such settings. We illustrate the method using the Weibull distribution and expect it to be applicable to other widely used lifetime distributions such as the loglogistic distribution. Our Simulation study show that the new approach provides better performance than existing methods when handling complete data and type-I censored data. Two numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the application of the proposed method. The proposed method is expected to be widely applicable in reliability engineering and survival analysis, offering a robust alternative to existing methods, particularly in scenarios involving censored data and small sample sizes.

entry.title: Inherited Local Shrinkage for Adaptive Functional Form Discovery

link.title: Inherited Local Shrinkage for Adaptive Functional Form Discovery

entry.content:
Statistical models frequently employ nonlinear effects, interactions, and multiresolution basis expansions to represent complex relationships between predictors and responses. Determining the appropriate level of model complexity, however, remains a fundamental challenge. This paper introduces \textit{Inherited Local Shrinkage} (ILS), a Bayesian global-local shrinkage framework for adaptive functional form discovery that incorporates strong heredity among hierarchically related predictors. ILS propagates shrinkage through directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) encoding relationships among predictors, allowing increasingly complex terms to contribute only when supported by their simpler ancestors. This construction provides a common prior framework for a broad class of hierarchical regression models. We demonstrate its application to polynomial regression, as well as multiresolution modeling with two-dimensional Haar wavelet and eigenvalue-ordered spline (EVOS) bases. Although these examples illustrate specific basis systems, ILS is not tied to any particular basis construction and can be applied to any regression model in which relationships among predictors can be represented by a DAG, regardless of the graph’s size or topology. Simulation studies demonstrate that ILS achieves competitive predictive performance relative to existing heredity-constrained methods while recovering underlying functional structure. Spatial applications further illustrate its ability to adaptively regulate model complexity across multiple resolutions, identifying where finer-scale detail is supported by the data. Together, these results establish ILS as a flexible framework for hierarchical complexity control and adaptive functional form discovery in Bayesian regression.
